paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the principal Appellant), her spouse, XXXX XXXX (the male Appellant), and their children, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX (the minor Appellants, respectively), all citizens of Republic of Nigeria, and XXXX XXXX XXXX, (a minor Appellant) a citizen of the United States of America, are appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claims for refugee protection. The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) assumes that the (male) Appellant has remained the designated representative (DR) for their minor children as the designation of the DR at the RPD is deemed to continue for a RAD appeal under RAD Rule 23(1). They have submitted no new evidence in support of their appeal. The Appellants ask the RAD to set aside the decision of the RPD and substitute its own positive decision, or to refer her claim to the RPD for redetermination by a differently-constituted panel.

Pursuant to subsection 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD that the Appellants are not Convention refugees nor are they persons in need of protection. The RAD dismisses the appeal. Background

The Appellants alleged before the RPD that family members of the male Appellant consider the principal Appellant and her daughter to be witches. The Appellants further allege before the RPD that as a result of this accusation they are being requested to undergo rituals, which include the females being subjected to Female Genital Mutilation (FGM). The Appellants further allege as a result they have a well-founded fear of persecution. The Appellants indicate that their Basis of Claim (BoC) form, narrative and supporting documents speak of their fear of persecution. The Appellants left Nigeria on XXXX XXXX, 2015 and made an inland claim for refugee protection on XXXX XXXX, 2015 in Canada.

The Appellants had their refugee determination hearings on December 21, 2015 and January 14, 2016. In a written decision issued on January 26, 2016 the RPD rejected the claims. The RPD member found that the male Appellant was excluded pursuant to Article 1F (b) and the other Appellants had a viable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Nigeria.
The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in its IFA analysis, that the RPD ignored or failed to take relevant evidence into consideration, and that the appeal can succeed on the basis of new evidence.

The Minister's representative, the "Minister", intervened in the RPD hearing asking the RPD to find that the male Appellant is an excluded person, pursuant to article 1F (b).1 The Minister did not intervene at the RAD. ANALYSIS The Role of the RAD
While the IRPA sets out grounds for appeal as well as possible remedies, it does not specify the standard by which the RAD is to review the decision of the lower tribunal.
The Appellants' counsel makes no submissions on the appropriate standard of review which is to be used by the RAD.
It is settled law that the RAD is not to review decisions of the RPD in the manner of a judicial review.2

The RAD is a statute of a different kind as is the appeal before it; its role and jurisdiction are best determined by looking at the legislative provisions creating the RAD and the appeal.3 Such an appeal: "(i) is directed at the decision of the RPD; (ii) unless new evidence is accepted, is to be entertained on the basis of the record as it was constituted at the time of the RPD's decision; and (iii) is to be concerned solely with the errors of law, of fact or of mixed fact and law that, according to the appellant, the RPD made. This is the statutory configuration of an appeal before the RAD."4

The Federal Court of Appeal in its decision clearly states, that the RAD is to carefully consider the RPD's decision and then carry out its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the Appellant, the RPD erred in its decision. The RAD is then to provide a final determination, either confirming the RPD's decision or setting it aside and substituting the RAD's own determination of the refugee claim. If the RAD cannot provide such a final determination without hearing the oral evidence already presented to the RPD, the matter can be referred back to the RPD.5

When the RAD is dealing with the findings of fact and of mixed fact and law, the RAD is to review the RPD's decision applying a standard of correctness.6 When applying that standard, the RAD will not show deference to the RPD's reasoning process; it will rather undertake its own analysis of the question. The analysis will bring the RAD to choose whether it agrees with the determination of the RPD; if not, then RAD will substitute its own view and provide the correct answer.7

However, there are cases where the RPD enjoys an expressive advantage over the RAD in making findings of fact or mixed fact and law, as such findings require an assessment of the credibility or weight to be given to oral evidence heard by the RPD.8 The Federal Court of Appeal, in deliberating the standard of review to be applied by the RAD to the RPD's decision, has declined to provide the scope and degree of deference to be shown by the RAD: "The RAD should be given the opportunity to develop its own jurisprudence in that respect; there is no need for me to pigeon-hole the RAD to the level of deference owed in each case."9

It is obvious from the reading of the Federal Court of Appeal decision that some level of deference is warranted, it is less evident how much deference is owed, and to what findings. As the Federal Court observed in Akuffo: "[T]here also appears to be a consensus that when no hearing is held before the RAD, the latter owes deference to the RPD's credibility findings. The opinions rather diverge on: i) the level of deference that is owed or its exact definition; and ii) the scope of the questions of fact and questions of mixed fact and law for which deference is owed."10

The RAD will show deference to the RPD's findings where the RPD was in an advantageous position to reach such conclusions. The RPD's advantage comes from seeing claimants and witnesses and hearing oral testimony from those individuals. Therefore, credibility findings which arise from that oral testimony are appropriate of deference, as are other findings of fact based on oral evidence, so are findings based on the RPD's specialized knowledge of a particular matter where the RAD does not have its own specialized knowledge with respect to the same factual issue. The RPD's advantage may even extend to personal documents in situations where it has questioned the claimant or witness about such documents and where the resulting testimony gives rise to credibility concerns.

The RAD notes that not every finding relating to credibility however, warrants deference. Where the RPD has made a finding of implausibility, for example, it has no advantage where the determination of plausibility is based on the RPD's own reasoning, or on objective documents, and does not arise directly from the oral evidence.11 Similarly, where the RPD draws an inference - a credibility finding based on deduction and reasoning, rather than a contradiction in evidence - here the RAD may see no reason to show deference, as the appellate tribunal can be expected to have equal expertise in the inferential process.12

The question becomes how much deference is owed by the RAD to findings of the RPD? In Huruglica, the Federal Court held that the RAD can "recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is a 'palpable and overriding error'."13 This passage has subsequently been endorsed by other decisions of the Federal Court.

It is unfortunate that the Federal Court did not explain what level of deference is established by recognizing and respecting a conclusion of the RPD, it has repeatedly upheld decisions in which the RAD applied a reasonableness standard to decisions of the RPD.14 This leads the RAD to believe, this proposes that "recognize and respect" is indeed somewhat similar to reasonableness.

In Dunsmuir, the Supreme Court discussed two elements of a deferential review: process and outcome.15 Despite the difference between judicial review and a RAD appeal, the RAD finds this framework helpful in considering its own approach to deference.

Where the RAD is to show deference to findings of the RPD, those findings must still be the result of an intelligible reasoning process. The RAD must be able to read the RPD's decision and comprehend how the RPD's conclusions were reached.

Additionally, the outcome of that process must be a product that is based on and supported by the evidence that was before the RPD. It is for this reason, that it is principally important that the RAD employ its own review of the evidence in the RPD's record, in order to conclude whether the RPD's outcome is supported by that evidence.

The RAD will apply a standard of correctness to its consideration of the RPD's decision: it will conduct its own review of the evidence and undertake its own analysis of the question. If this does not lead the RAD to the same conclusion as the RPD, the RPD's finding is wrong.

But the RAD will not interfere with the RPD's findings where such conclusions result from the RPD's distinct advantages or from a intelligible reasoning process whose premises are embedded in such advantages. If either the process or the conclusion does not meet these requirements, the RAD will determine the findings to be in error.

Having done this, the RAD will provide a final determination, either by confirming the RPD's decision or setting it aside and substituting its own determination. If it cannot do so without hearing oral evidence that was already heard by the RPD, it will refer the matter back for redetermination. ANALYSIS OF THE EVIDENCE In regards to the Exclusion 1F (b)

The Appellants argue that the Panel erred in its analysis of the exclusion clause under Article 1F (b). The Panel determined that the male Appellant was excluded from protection as there were serious reasons for considering that the Appellant committed a serious non-political crime.16

The burden is on the Minister to make a case for exclusion before the RPD that the Appellant is excluded from refugee protection pursuant to section 98 of the IRPA and Section F(b) of Article 1 of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees ("Article 1F(b)").17

The Minister also submitted that the Appellant's testimony and documentary evidence regarding his arrest in the United States of America for Fraud and Use, trafficking or possession of forged document supports a finding of serious reasons for considering that the claimant has committed a serious, non-political crime, as found in section 380, section 368 and section 403 (1) of the Criminal Code of Canada [CCC].
The Appellant's counsel in submissions stated that a finding of exclusion on such basis is not supportable, his actions were not serious within the context of Article 1F (b).18

I disagree with the Appellants' submission that "conviction for Fraud and Use, trafficking or possession of forged document," is not a serious offence. The fact that the penalty for Fraud carries a maximum of 14 years and the other two carry maximum penalties of 10 years, this strongly suggests that Canada does consider such crimes to be "serious". As stated by the Federal Court of Appeal in Jayasekara,19 "while regard should be had to international standards, the perspective of the receiving state or nation cannot be ignored in determining the seriousness of the crime". Thus, the Court noted that there is a strong indication in the IRPA that Canada, as a receiving state, considers crimes for which an offence may be punishable by a maximum term of at least 10 years to be a "serious" crime. By logical corollary, the fact that the crimes of Fraud and Use, trafficking or possession of forged document is punishable by a maximum sentence of fourteen years for Fraud and ten years for the other two strongly suggests that they are crimes that Canada considers to be "serious".

The Minister argues that on the facts presently before the RAD as they were before the RPD, there is sufficient evidence to support a finding of exclusion by the Panel for serious criminality under Article 1F (b), such that there are reasonable grounds to believe the Appellant committed an act outside Canada, before entering Canada, that constitutes a serious, excludable crime. The RAD has assessed the evidence in this area and finds that the male Appellant was convicted in the USA in the State of Massachusetts on "credit card fraud" and sentenced to 20 months in prison, three years' probation and pay restitution in the amount of $14,020.
The RPD provided very clear and fulsome reasons20 on how it arrived at its finding. The RAD has assessed the RPD findings and concurs with the RPD findings.

I also note that the RPD had serious concerns about the credibility of the adult Appellants regarding their dealings with filing police reports. The RPD stated in its reasons: The panel also finds that the claimant omitted from his narrative that he later called a friend who is a police commissioner XXXX who confirmed to the male claimant that he issued of FGM is a family matter and the police would not investigate matter.21

Based on the foregoing, the RAD concurs with the RPD's finding that there is sufficient credible evidence on which to find that the male Appellant is an excluded person due to alleged serious non-political criminality prior to his entry into Canada.
The RAD finds that the male Appellant is an excluded person, as per Article 1F (b) and section 98 of the IRPA.
The RPD found that the Appellants have a reasonable IFA in Abuja, Benin State or Port Harcourt. The Appellants plead that the RPD should have carried out a thorough analysis of their subjective fear.

The RAD does not agree with the Appellants. When assessing the viability of an IFA, the RPD must apply a two-pronged test. The RPD followed this approach. The basis for this two-pronged test is the cases of Rasaratnam22 and Thirunavukkarasu.23
The Board must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists.24

Conditions in that part of the country considered being an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all circumstances, including those particular to the claimant, for him or her to seek refuge there.25
The RAD will apply this two-pronged approach The First Prong of the IFA The Appellants' elderly uncle, the agents of persecution

The RPD found that the Appellant did not disclose any supporting documentation to establish that the Appellants' elderly uncle, the agents of persecution, is well-known public figures in Nigeria who wield any degree of influence of power in Nigeria. In particular, the RPD found that the Appellant provided no documentation to support the allegation that his elderly uncle is a popular and public figure in Nigeria who consults as an herbalist with politicians, police officers and military officers. The RPD found that the Appellants provided no documentary evidence to establish that his elderly uncle who has the wealth or connections to the police.

The Appellants referred to the jurisprudence, in which the Federal Court of Appeal, in Maldonado,26 states that when a claimant swears that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are true unless there is valid reason to doubt their truthfulness. The Appellants plead that the RPD did not provide valid reasons to doubt the truthfulness of the influence of the agents of persecution. The Appellants also referred to the jurisprudence where the Federal Court has warned against rejecting a claim based solely on the lack of corroborative evidence.27
The Appellants plead that the RPD had no reason to doubt the Appellant's evidence on the point surrounding their photographs being furnished to police in Nigeria.
The RAD agrees with the RPD for the following reasons.

The RAD finds, for the following reasons, that in the case at hand, corroborative evidence can be reasonably expected. The Basis of Claim (BOC) form clearly instructs the Appellants to provide "any documents you have to support your claim".28 According to the Appellant's BOC narrative and his oral testimony before the RPD, the Appellant had contact with family members in Nigeria after he arrived in Canada. The Appellant had sometime before his hearings to obtain documentary evidence regarding the agents of persecution, yet there was no evidence adduced that they made any attempts to obtain any supporting evidence. Given the size of Nigeria both in area and population, an area of over 900,000 square kilometers and a population of over 180 million,29 the RAD finds it critical to establish the profile of agents of persecution who could find the Appellants in Nigeria.

According to the recording of the hearing, the Appellant testified that his elderly uncle as other members of his family relied upon him giving them money. This evidence clearly indicates that the male Appellant's family lacks the resources to be able to have any authority with the police or anyone else to conduct a search for the whereabouts of the Appellants. The male Appellant did not provide any evidence of his uncle's profile such as his work and status in the country. No evidence was adduced if he had made any efforts to obtain evidence regarding his elderly uncle, the Appellant testified that he tried but got no one. The RAD finds these responses or lack of were vague and provide no information regarding efforts made to obtain evidence and why the efforts were not fruitful. The RPD asked the Appellant how his uncle and family might find the Appellants if they were in Port Harcourt, a city with millions of people. The Appellant testified that he sometimes appeared on television, but did not directly answer the question. The RAD finds this response did not address the question adequately. The RAD is entitled to reject some or all of the inferences drawn by an Appellant, especially if they are speculative in nature, even in the absence of an adverse finding of credibility.30

According to the recording of the hearing the Appellant testified that he is known throughout Nigeria as he sometimes appears on television, but provided nothing to support this. The Appellant explained that his uncle and family reside in Ibadan but not how he would be able to trace them anywhere in Nigeria. In addition, having listened to the recording of the hearing, the RAD founds the Appellant's testimony regarding his uncle ability to trace them to be lacking in sufficient detail. The RPD asked the Appellant how the elderly uncle would find the Appellants if they resided in Abuja, or Port Harcourt. The Appellant testified that due to his business he would have to work and the children would have to attend school, further if it became known that his wife was a witch, they would be killed. The RAD finds this explanation unsatisfactory, as the questions was not adequately answered. The RAD finds it highly unlikely that people in Port Harcourt or Abuja would know or recognize the Appellants in the IFAs, as the allegation of the principal Appellant being a witch is a local issue. The people of Port Harcourt or Abuja would not know anything about the allegation against the principal Appellant unless they were told by the Appellants.

The RAD finds, on the basis of the evidence before it, that the Appellants have not established, on a balance of probabilities, that they would be tracked down or targeted in Abuja, or Port Harcourt. Given the lack of evidence presented related to the influence and reach of the elderly uncles, the agent of persecution, the RAD finds that the Appellants have not adduced sufficient evidence to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that there is a serious possibility of being persecuted in the IFA cities or that they would be personally subjected to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in Abuja, or Port Harcourt.
The RAD has, therefore, considered the interest and the ability of the Nigerian Police Force (NPF) to apprehend the Appellants in the IFA locales.

The Appellants have been out of Nigeria for over one year. They provided no persuasive evidence that they have high profiles and no persuasive evidence that the NPF are looking for them throughout the country. There is no persuasive evidence that there is a large resourceful group of people in Nigeria, a country of over 180 million31 people, who are searching of would continue to search for the Appellants and seek them out in Abuja, or Port Harcourt. The RAD notes that the population of Abuja is more than 2.5 million.

A report from the United Kingdom Home Office states that the 1999 Nigerian constitution provides for the freedom of movement within Nigeria, and states that every citizen of Nigeria is entitled to move freely throughout Nigeria and to reside in any part thereof, and no citizen of Nigeria shall be expelled from Nigeria or refused entry thereto or exit therefrom.32 There are international airports in Abuja and Port Harcourt. The RAD notes the obvious fact that the Nigerian authorities do not have to be advised about the Appellants' return to the country and would, therefore, have no knowledge of their whereabouts in any of these cities. In any case, if the Appellants do not wish to inform others of their presence in any of the IFAs, there is no reason to believe that their location would be found out. Thus, the Appellants have failed to provide a reasonable explanation as to why they believe they would be discovered and/or harmed in any of the three IFAs.

The Appellants provided no persuasive evidence that they are a matter of nation-wide interest to the NPF. The RAD is not persuaded that the NPF throughout the country are searching for the Appellants. Nevertheless, the RAD considered the documentary evidence regarding the NPF. A report from the UK Home Office indicates that the NPF is the principal law enforcement agency in Nigeria with more than 350,000 men and women. NPF is a federal police force covering all 36 Nigerian states and the federal capital territory, Abuja. The report states that a serious lack of resources, including communications equipment, vehicles, skilled leadership, and training, continued to undermine the effectiveness of the NPF. There have been reports of police asking victims of crime to provide vehicles for transportation, or money to buy fuel for police vehicles.33 A recent Response to Information Request (RIR)34 provides information regarding the poor funding for the NPF which has led to low morale amongst serving officers. The same RIR indicates that the police lack office space, personnel, and facilities for effective performance of its functions. According to another RIR,35 the IG of Police reportedly stated that one of the greatest challenges police are facing in Nigeria is a lack of adequate communication equipment. The IG of police also indicated that material inputs in terms of funding, crime prevention/control, detection, investigation, traffic-control and accident prevention, communication and data-gathering research needs are inadequate. The RAD is not persuaded that the Nigerian police are competent and well enough equipped or motivated to search for the Appellants throughout the country.

Thus, the Appellants have failed to provide a reasonable explanation as to why they believe they would be discovered and/or harmed by the NPF in Abuja, or Port Harcourt. Therefore, the RAD finds that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellants could live in any of these three cities without serious possibility of persecution.
The RAD has reviewed the RPD's analysis and the evidence which supports its findings and agrees with the findings made. The Second Prong of the IFA
The RAD concurs with the RPD for the following reasons. The Appellant's psychological condition
The RAD conducted its own assessment of the psychological report36 of psychologist Dr. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, dated XXXX XXXX, 2015.

Dr. XXXX states that the Appellants satisfied diagnostic criteria for stressor-related disorder with prolonged duration. The RAD accepts the diagnosis of the psychologist. However, the RAD gives little weight to the document as it relates to the viability of an IFA for the Appellants. The Appellant's mental state does not affect the RAD's conclusions in this regard. The RAD's reasons follow.

Dr. XXXX states that the psychological assessment was completed to accompany the Appellant's request to stay in Canada. Dr. XXXX states that the Appellant requires mental-health treatment but that, as of the date of the report, the Appellant had received no such treatment. The Appellant provided no evidence that he sought mental-health care after his interview with Dr. XXXX which was conducted nine months before his hearings before the RPD. The RAD, therefore, has no reason to believe that the report was written in the context of an on-going therapeutic relationship between the author and the Appellant. The Appellant's own actions in not seeking treatment for his mental health do not suggest that he takes seriously the diagnosis in the report.

Dr. XXXX provided the following information: Mr. XXXX (the Appellant's) satisfies diagnostic criteria for post trauma stress disorder (309.81[F43.10] with dissociative symptoms in the American Psychiatric Association's Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed., DSM-5). He requires mental-health treatment. Psychological treatment might include stress-management training, behavioral activation, and cognitive-behaviour therapy. Mr. XXXX condition will deteriorate with exposure to further threats of harm.37

The RAD finds this information has no probative value. There is nothing in the report to show that other than the 60 minutes that the male Appellant and the principal Appellant met with the doctor, no other sessions have taken place nor is there any evidence on any ongoing treatment. It is clear that the entire assessment of both the male Appellant and the principal Appellant took place over a 60 minute session. There is no evidence before the RAD that the Appellants have been given any future treatment, what can be deciphered from the report is that neither Appellant are in any treatment programs. As such the RAD finds little probative value in the report of Dr. XXXX.

The RAD has also considered the documentary evidence provided by the Appellants with regard to medical care available to the Appellant in Nigeria. The UK Home Office report of June 14, 2013 (reissued February 3, 2014) indicates that mental health services are limited in Nigeria and often underutilized because of widespread ignorance and supernatural beliefs about the etiology of mental illness. Psychiatric care is provided at a few large mental hospitals in big cities. Nigeria's mental health facilities consist of eight federally funded psychiatric hospitals and six state-owned mental hospitals and managed by various state governments. Primary Care Prescription regulations authorize primary health care doctors and nurses to prescribe and/or continue prescriptions for psychotherapeutic medicines. The report lists over thirty mental health drugs available in Nigeria.38
The RAD, therefore, finds that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellants could access adequate mental-health care in Abuja, or Port Harcourt if they so choose. The wife's relocation

The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to apply the Chairperson Guidelines and this is a breach of natural justice. The RAD fully disagrees with this argument, and finds that the RPD provide fulsome and clear reasons on its application of the Chairpersons Guidelines.39 The RAD finds that the RPD did not commit a breach of natural justice in this respect as it clearly addressed both the Women's - Gender and the Children Refugee Guidelines.

The RPD found that the Appellant and his wife were well educated and had good employment potential and could, thus provide for themselves and the minor Appellants in the IFA locales. The RPD referred to a number of documents found within the NDP which refer specifically to women and female children relocating within Nigeria who require physical protection. The RPD found that there are resources available to vulnerable women and female children such as the wife and minor female Appellant facing forced circumcision.

The Appellants argue that the RPD did not pay due consideration to particular documentary evidence which speaks to the challenges of relocation for women in Nigeria. The Appellants referred to documentary evidence which indicates, for example, that women may be stigmatized in their new communities due to social and cultural constraints or that a woman who chooses to relocate could face a number of economic and social constraints depending upon her situation.

The RAD agrees with the RPD. The documentary evidence referred to by the Appellants in this regard refers specifically to the problems encountered by women relocating on their own or with their children, not a woman relocating with her husband. The RAD finds that the Appellants have conflated the situation with women in Nigeria relocating on their own with the Appellants' situation where the wife would be relocating with her husband, the Appellant, and the minor Appellants. The RAD notes that the male Appellant would be present and as such he would also be protective of the principal Appellant and the minor Appellants.

Therefore, the RAD notes as per the RPD finding that the Appellants could live in any of the two cities without fear or the need to hide. If the Appellants do not wish to inform others of their presence in these cities, there is no reason to believe that their location would be found out. The RAD notes that the cities are large and located at a substantial distance from Lagos.
Based on the totality of the evidence, the RAD notes that the record contained sufficient evidence to support a finding that an IFA in Abuja or Port Harcourt is accessible to the Appellants.

The RAD finds the RPD finding that on a balance of probabilities, that there is not a serious possibility of persecution of the Appellants in these cities, that their removal to Nigeria would not subject them personally to a risk to his life, or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture. The RAD finds that the Appellants have failed to provide sufficient evidence as to why they believe they would be discovered and/or harmed at any of these locations, and therefore there is no reason to believe, on a balance of probabilities, that they would be harmed.

The RAD assessed the RPD's finding in regard to the reasonableness of the IFA in Abuja or Port Harcourt. The test for reasonableness is whether it would be unduly harsh to expect the claimants to move to another, less hostile part of the country before seeking status abroad, as per Thirunavukkarasu.40 This requires an evaluation of the conditions in the IFA as well as the Appellants or similarly situated persons. Thirunavukkarasu sets a very high threshold for what makes an IFA unreasonable in all the circumstances. The hardship associated with dislocation and relocation is not the kind of undue hardship that renders an IFA unreasonable.41 However, it is not enough for the Appellant to say that he or she does not like the weather there, or that he or she has no friends or relatives there, or that he or she may not be able to find suitable work there.42
In considering the viability of the IFA, the RPD has given consideration to the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines,43 specifically as it relates to IFA. The Guidelines state in part:

In determining the reasonableness of a woman's recourse to an internal flight alternative, decision-makers should consider the ability of women, because of their gender, to travel safely to the IFA and to stay there without facing undue hardship.

The RAD also considered counsel's submissions in the Appellants' memorandum in which he argued that there is no protection against gender-based violence in Nigeria. The RAD takes note that the female Appellant has received and continues to receive strong support from her husband. He has demonstrated a commitment to the principal Appellant throughout the situation, and there is no reason to believe that he will not continue to provide her with ongoing support. In light of that, the RAD finds that any hardship encountered by the principal Appellant arising from her gender will be mitigated by the fact that she will receive support from her husband.

The Appellants provided no persuasive evidence that they would not be familiar with cultural issues and norms in these cities. Therefore, the RAD is satisfied that it would be reasonable for the Appellants to adapt to new surroundings in any of these cities and be able to obtain employment in her respective areas. In addition, although most Nigerians depend upon their family, relying on immediate and extended family is not the only option. Many Nigerians try to establish other support networks that may complement or in some cases replace the extended family. Examples of such support networks are religious congregations, religious organizations, age grades/sets, political organizations, charities and guilds. Many such organizations are expected to aid their members in ways that would be fairly unusual in a western context. The Appellants testified that they are practicing Christians. The documentary evidence states that the southern states of Nigeria (in which Ibadan is located) are predominantly Christian while both Muslims and Christians reside in large numbers in the Federal Capital Territory where Abuja is found. For this reason, the RAD is satisfied that the Appellants have sources of moral and spiritual assistance and support available to them in Nigeria.

Given the finding above that the principal Appellant and the minor Appellants have an internal flight alternative in Nigeria, the RAD finds that the principal Appellant and the minor Appellants do not face a serious possibility of persecution there, and it also finds that their removal to Nigeria would not subject them personally to a risk to life, or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture.
The RAD finds that the Appellants have a viable IFA in Abuja, or Port Harcourt. Minor Claimant

With respect to the child born in the U.S., namely, XXXX XXXX XXXX, as he is a citizen of the United States, he enjoys the rights and privileges of that country. He would be able to benefit from the social safety networks of the U.S. and the U.S. would be able to extend protection to this child who is a national of that country.

Furthermore, counsel has not provided any evidence against the United States claiming persecution should he return, the RAD also notes that there is no claim against the U.S., who would protect him if he was in need of protection.
Therefore, I find that the minor child born in the U.S. is neither a Convention refugee, nor is he a person in need of protection. Therefore, I am rejecting his appeal.
The RAD finds the male Appellant is excluded as per Article 1F (b).
The RAD finds that the principal Appellants and XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX (the minor Appellants) have a viable internal flight alternative in Nigeria.
The RAD finds XXXX XXXX XXXX, minor Appellant born in the U.S. is neither a Convention refugee, nor is he a person in need of protection.
The RAD finds that the Appellants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection and dismisses the appeal in accordance with section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.

The RAD dismisses the appeal. (signed) "Luis F. Agostinho" Luis F.
